channel.title: Road Guide: Day 2 quicker route
channel.description: Day 2 quicker: Guerneville → Jenner → Bodega Bay → Valley Ford → Petaluma → US 101 → Muir Woods → Golden Gate → SFO. Play episodes in order as you drive.
channel.itunes:author: Wine Country Road Guide

item.title: 01. Korbel: Bohemian brothers and California champagne
item.description:
Okay, wine lovers, up ahead is a winery that legally prints the word champagne on its labels, and France can't do anything about it.
It's Korbel, making sparkling wine here since 1882. It was started by Francis Korbel and his brothers, who came from Bohemia, and who also, randomly, started a satirical San Francisco magazine called The Wasp. They use the proper Champagne method, where the wine gets its second fermentation right in the bottle you buy.
So how do they get away with saying champagne? … Old American rules from the 1930s treat some place names as semi-generic, as long as the label

item.title: 02. Rio Nido: there is no Canyon Five
item.description:
Here's one of my favourite little places: Rio Nido, the river nest, a tiny resort village tucked into a redwood canyon. It was started in 1908 by a San Francisco lodge called the Eagles, so its first name was Eaglenest. In World War Two, its dance hall was packed with sailors on leave and big bands played there.
Okay, Julia, Adam, here's a weird one. The streets here are named Canyon One, Canyon Two, Canyon Three, Canyon Four, then Canyon Six and Canyon Seven. What's missing? … There's no Canyon Five! The story goes it's because of an accident on the road that became Canyon Six. Spooky.

item.title: 03. Guerneville: from Stumptown to resort town
item.description:
Ladies and gentlemen, Julia, Adam and our amazing driver: welcome to Guerneville! You made it! Woohoo!
Okay, pronunciation check. It's Gurn-vill. Locals even sell T-shirts that say Don't call it Guerneyville. So now you know.
Final quiz of the trip. The town's very first English name was a bit less pretty. Given that loggers cut down most of the giant redwoods here in the late 1800s, what do you think they called it? … Stumptown! And the parade every year is still called Stumptown Days. The redwoods grew so thick here that local legend says the valley had the densest amount of living stuff o

item.title: 04. Armstrong Redwoods: the trees the loggers missed
item.description:
If you've got an hour, go see the trees that the loggers missed: Armstrong Redwoods, just north of town. In the 1870s, Colonel James Armstrong saved the grove as a natural park. After he died, his daughter and another local family ran a whole campaign, with rallies and car caravans, to save this last bit of the old forest, and in 1917 the county bought it for 80,000 dollars.
Quiz: the tallest tree in there, the Parson Jones Tree, is a hundred yards from the entrance. How tall do you think it is? … More than 310 feet! That's taller than a thirty-storey building. And the oldest, the Colonel Arm

item.title: 05. The Pomo: the people of the Russian River
item.description:
This river is Pomo country. The Pomo lands once stretched from the Pacific coast all the way inland to Clear Lake. But here's the thing: the Pomo were never one single nation. They lived in small, independent bands linked by family, and they spoke seven related languages so different that speakers of one couldn't understand another.
Quiz: the name Pomo was originally the name of just one village. What do you think it meant? … Those who live at red earth hole! Probably after the red magnesite they mined to make beads, or the reddish soil. By 1877, English speakers were using it for everyone.

item.title: 06. Day two: river, ocean, redwoods, bridge
item.description:
Good morning, road-trippers! Julia, Adam, our heroic driver: welcome to day two. And what a day. We're following the Russian River all the way to the ocean. Then it's down the wild Sonoma Coast to Bodega Bay, where Alfred Hitchcock made birds terrifying. After that, either along Tomales Bay and the Point Reyes coast, or inland through Petaluma, to the giant redwoods of Muir Woods. Then over the Golden Gate Bridge and through San Francisco to the airport.
Quick warm-up quiz while you finish your coffee. Today we're going to cross the biggest, most famous fault line in America, more than once.

item.title: 07. Bohemian Grove: the most exclusive campsite in America
item.description:
Okay, conspiracy fans, this one's for you. Just downstream at Monte Rio, hidden in the redwoods, is the Bohemian Grove: a 2,700-acre private campground owned by San Francisco's very exclusive Bohemian Club. Every July, powerful people from politics, business and the arts spend more than two weeks camping here.
It started innocently. In 1878, a bunch of journalists from the club had an overnight going-away party in the redwoods for an actor moving to New York. They had so much fun they did it again the next year, without him! Then the rich businessmen joined, and the money and the power follow

item.title: 08. The Russians in California
item.description:
We've met Russians again and again today: a river, a mountain, a farm near Graton. So here's the whole story.
Russian traders pushed east across Siberia and the North Pacific, and in 1799 they set up a colony in Alaska. Their business was fur, especially sea otters. From 1803, American ship captains took Alaska Native hunters down the California coast to hunt otters, and between 1805 and 1812 alone they gathered over 22,000 pelts.
In 1812 the Russians built their own base, Fort Ross, on the Sonoma coast, in the land of the Kashaya Pomo. It was super diverse: Native Californians, Native Alask

item.title: 09. Cannabis: California's other crop
item.description:
Wine isn't the only crop around here with a complicated legal history.
California has been at the front of cannabis politics for half a century. In 1972, it held the first ballot vote in the nation to legalise cannabis. Quiz: did it pass? … Nope! It failed. But in 1996, California became the first state to legalise medical cannabis, and in 2016, voters legalised recreational use, with 57 percent of the vote.
Legalisation turned out to be messy. Growers had to register and get permits, and more than half of the medical dispensaries closed. Legal businesses pay hefty taxes, while illegal growe

item.title: 10. Monte Rio and Duncans Mills: the railroad to the redwoods
item.description:
Picture this road with a little narrow-gauge train chugging along beside the river. From the 1870s, the North Pacific Coast Railroad ran from Cazadero, through Monte Rio and Duncans Mills, all the way down to the Sausalito ferry. And you'll hear its name again and again today, because it also stopped at Valley Ford, Tomales, Marshall and Point Reyes Station.
At first it hauled redwood lumber to build San Francisco. In 1877 Alexander Duncan set up a sawmill right here, and the town grew up around it, with two hotels, a saloon, a blacksmith and a livery stable. When the mills moved on, the trai

item.title: 11. Goat Rock: sea stacks, mammoths and the Goonies
item.description:
Okay, movie quiz! Down on the left is Goat Rock Beach, with that huge flat-topped rock barely hanging on to the land. In 1985, a very famous adventure movie, about a group of kids hunting for pirate treasure, filmed its ending on this beach. Which movie? … The Goonies! Goonies never say die.
Now look at all those rocks sticking out of the sea. They're called sea stacks, and here's how they got there. For about 170 million years, an ocean plate was diving under North America. It scraped off pillow lava, chert and sandstone, and crushed it all into mélange, which is a jumble of hard blocks floa

item.title: 12. Jenner: the river meets the sea, and a pump made of gold
item.description:
There it is! The Russian River meets the Pacific Ocean, right here at Jenner. Population: about a hundred and twenty.
Quick reminder of why it's called the Russian River. Russians from the Russian-American Company explored it in the early 1800s, when they set up Fort Ross, about ten miles up the coast. They called it the Slavyanka. The Pomo had much older names for it, including Bidapte, big river.
The town is named after Dr. Elijah Jenner, a dentist and inventor from Vermont who came west for the Gold Rush in 1850. While he was mining, he designed a pump that could lift water a hundred feet

item.title: 13. Seventeen miles of wild coast
item.description:
This is the Sonoma Coast, seventeen miles of state beaches running all the way down to Bodega Head. Little coves, big rocks, cliffs, and fog that can roll in fast.
Quiz: those bluffs are made of soft soil, and the ocean's chewing away at them. How much land do you think this coast loses in an average year? … One to three feet a year! More in a stormy winter. It's also rising. Over the ages this land has been pushed up, which is why you're driving on a flat shelf above the beach. It's called a marine terrace: old sea floor, lifted up. Some of those sea stacks are even standing up on the terrac

item.title: 14. Bodega Bay: Russians, Spaniards and a lot of movies
item.description:
Welcome to Bodega Bay! Fishing boats, salty air, and a harbor tucked behind that long headland.
The bay is named after Juan Francisco de la Bodega y Quadra, a Spanish naval officer who sailed in here in 1775. In 1793 the Spanish sent a little garrison with four cannons, because they'd heard the English might show up. They didn't, so the guns went back to Monterey. And then guess who did show up? The Russians! In 1809, before they built Fort Ross, they put up the first Russian buildings in California here, and called it Port Rumyantsev, after their foreign minister.
Hollywood loves this town.

item.title: 15. The Birds: Hitchcock terrorises Bodega Bay
item.description:
Okay, The Birds! In 1963, Alfred Hitchcock made a horror film about birds suddenly, inexplicably attacking the people of Bodega Bay. Tippi Hedren, in her first film, plays a San Francisco socialite who drives up here with a pair of lovebirds, and things go very badly. Gulls at the dock, crows at the schoolhouse, sparrows pouring down the chimney.
Quiz: Hitchcock was partly inspired by a real event in 1961, when thousands of seabirds dive-bombed a California seaside town called Capitola, crashing into cars and dropping half-eaten fish on people's lawns. Gross. What do you think really caused i

item.title: 16. The Hole in the Head: the nuclear plant that never was
item.description:
Across the harbor is Bodega Head, and it has a hole in it. Literally. Here's the story.
In the late 1950s and early 60s, the utility company PG&E planned to build a nuclear power plant on Bodega Head. It was meant to be the first commercially viable nuclear plant in the United States. The fishermen were worried about their livelihoods. And a local woman, Rose Gaffney, who owned land on the headland, refused to sell, sued the company, and invited government officials to come and see the fault lines on the site for themselves.
Quiz: in June 1963, the protesters released 1,500 of something into

item.title: 17. Bodega: rusty cannons and a famous schoolhouse
item.description:
This little village is Bodega, once called Bodega Corners, to tell it apart from the port down by the water. There used to be two Coast Miwok villages in the area. Then the Russians settled in the Salmon Creek valley here in 1809.
Quiz: around 1843, John Sutter bought land from the departing Russians, including this area. What did the deal include? Guess one thing. … Some hunting rights, a small boat, several rusty cannons and some old muskets! What a bargain.
In 1843 a Captain Stephen Smith also built the first lumber mill on the West Coast near here. Then the town proper began in 1853 with

item.title: 18. Valley Ford and the Running Fence
item.description:
Tiny Valley Ford, population about a hundred and fifty. Dairy country: rolling green hills and cows.
The Coast Miwok had a village here called Ewapalt. In the 1850s there was a grain mill, and from 1876 the North Pacific Coast Railroad stopped here, so ranchers and fishers could ship their produce down to San Francisco.
Quiz: in 1976, a famous pair of artists, Christo and Jeanne-Claude, built a giant artwork that passed right through Valley Ford, running from Cotati all the way to Bodega Bay. What do you think it was? … A fence! Running Fence: a long white fabric fence across the hills, all

item.title: 19. The Coast Miwok
item.description:
The land from the Golden Gate up to the Sonoma coast, and east to Sonoma Creek, was home to the Coast Miwok. That includes the hills around Sebastopol and Freestone and the lower Sonoma Valley.
They lived in small bands with no central government. In spring they headed to the coast for salmon, shellfish and seaweed. The rest of the year, acorns were the staple, plus deer and rabbit. Quiz: Coast Miwok hunters had a clever trick for sneaking up on deer. What do you think they did? … They rubbed themselves with a plant called Brewer's angelica to hide their scent! They also drank yerba buena tea

item.title: 20. Petaluma: the Egg Capital of the World
item.description:
Welcome to Petaluma! Quiz: Petaluma's old nickname was the Egg Capital of the World. And it had another nickname, a pun on the name. Can you guess it? … Chickaluma! This town was all about chickens. It had the only known poultry drugstore, a pharmacy for chickens. And in 1879, Lyman Byce invented the coal-lamp egg incubator here. They still celebrate with a Butter and Eggs Day parade.
The land was part of Rancho Petaluma, given in 1834 to our old friend General Vallejo from Sonoma. In 1836 he built a huge adobe ranch house just east of town, the largest privately owned adobe ever built in Cal

item.title: 21. Chief Marin and the naming of Marin County
item.description:
We're coming through San Rafael, the county seat of Marin. So who was Marin?
The Coast Miwok have lived in Marin for about 6,500 years, and more than 600 of their village sites have been found. According to General Vallejo, who chaired the committee that named California's counties in 1850, this county was named after Marin, a great Coast Miwok chief. His birth name was Huicmuse. He was baptized Marino at about the age of twenty, in 1801, and lived at Mission Dolores in San Francisco for years, often serving as godfather at baptisms. Vallejo believed he'd fought fierce battles against the Spa

item.title: 22. Muir Woods: the man who gave away a forest
item.description:
Welcome to Muir Woods, one of the last old-growth redwood forests in the Bay Area. It's a narrow canyon on the slope of Mount Tam, wrapped in summer fog, which these trees drink up during the dry season.
Here's how it survived. Mount Tam's redwoods were logged heavily to build San Francisco, and again to rebuild it after 1906. But the trees in this canyon, then called Redwood Canyon, were too hard to reach. In 1905, William Kent and his wife Elizabeth bought 611 acres of it for 45,000 dollars, with money borrowed from a banker friend, to save it. Then a water company tried to take part of it

item.title: 23. Muir Woods and the founding of the United Nations
item.description:
One more Muir Woods story. In April 1945, delegates from 50 countries gathered in San Francisco to write the Charter of the United Nations. President Franklin Roosevelt was supposed to open the conference, but he died on the 12th of April, just before it started. So on the 19th of May, the delegates came out here to Cathedral Grove and held a ceremony in his memory, among the redwoods, and placed a plaque in his honor. It's still there.
And a practical note: Muir Woods gets up to six thousand visitors a day at busy times, and parking is so limited that since 2018 you need a reservation to par

item.title: 24. Coast redwoods: the tallest living things on Earth
item.description:
Let's talk about the coast redwood, Sequoia sempervirens. Quiz: how tall do you think the tallest living redwood is? … About 381 feet! That's the tallest living tree on Earth, way up in Humboldt County. They can live about 2,000 years, and the trunks can be 29 feet across.
Redwoods have been around a very long time. Their relatives' fossils go back to the age of the dinosaurs. They only grow in a narrow strip along the coast, from Big Sur up to the corner of Oregon, because they need that fog. In the dry summers, they drink moisture straight out of the fog.

item.title: 25. Mill Valley, Chief Marin and the Blind Pig
item.description:
This junction, where Highway 1 meets 101, is at the edge of Mill Valley, the town tucked into the redwood canyons on the side of Mount Tam.
People have lived here a very long time. Fourteen Coast Miwok village sites have been found in the Mill Valley area, with huge shell mounds along Richardson Bay. One mound, excavated in 1907, was twenty feet high. And a plaque in a Mill Valley sidewalk marks the spot believed to be the birthplace of Chief Marin, in 1781.
Quiz: right around this intersection, in 1916, a roadhouse was built that became famous during Prohibition. It was called the Blind Pig

item.title: 26. Sausalito: streets under the bay
item.description:
Down to the left is Sausalito, on Richardson Bay. The name is Spanish for small willow grove, and it's been spelled about a dozen different ways over the years.
Before the bridge, Sausalito was the end of the line: trains from up north, including that North Pacific Coast Railroad from the Russian River, met the ferries here. The car ferry to San Francisco took about twenty minutes and cost a dollar per car. In World War Two it became a shipbuilding center, and afterwards it turned arty and wealthy, famous for its houseboats.
Quiz: when Sausalito was laid out, planners assumed the town would

item.title: 27. The Marin Headlands: the city that never got built
item.description:
Those wild green hills on your right, at the very tip of Marin, are the Marin Headlands. They look untouched, but they came close to being a city.
Quiz: in the 1960s, the government sold more than 2,000 acres here to a developer who planned a whole new city called Marincello. How many people do you think it was meant for? … 30,000! In 50 apartment towers, with houses, a shopping center and a hotel. In 1970 the developer lost a lawsuit, and the land was sold to the Golden Gate National Recreation Area instead. Phew.
The headlands are dotted with old forts and gun batteries from the 1890s thro

item.title: 28. The Golden Gate Bridge
item.description:
Here it is, everybody! The Golden Gate Bridge! Cameras up, passengers!
It opened in 1937, and at that point it was the longest and tallest suspension bridge in the world. The towers are 746 feet tall, and the main span is 4,200 feet. Lots of experts said it couldn't be built, because of the wind, the fog, and the swirling tides.
Quiz: the colour is called International Orange, chosen by the architect Irving Morrow. But the U.S. Navy had a different suggestion, to make it more visible to ships. What do you think the Navy wanted? … Black and yellow stripes! Like a giant bumblebee. Thank goodne

item.title: 29. Roller skates, bankers and a flattened bridge
item.description:
A few more bridge stories. During the Depression, the bridge district couldn't sell its bonds to pay for construction. Then in 1932, Amadeo Giannini, the founder of Bank of America, bought the whole lot himself, to help the local economy.
The day before cars were allowed on it, in May 1937, 200,000 people walked across. Some on roller skates! And for the fiftieth birthday in 1987, they closed it to cars again. Up to a million people showed up, around 300,000 crammed onto the bridge at once, and the curve in the middle of the deck actually flattened out under their weight. Engineers say it was

item.title: 30. The Presidio: from Spanish fort to Lucasfilm
item.description:
Off the end of the bridge we're driving through the Presidio, a big wooded park that was a military base for 219 years.
The Spanish founded it on the 17th of September, 1776. That's the same year as the American Declaration of Independence, on the other side of the continent. Then it passed to Mexico, then in 1848 to the U.S. Army, and in 1994 the Army handed it to the National Park Service. Congress told the Presidio to pay for itself, and it did, eight years early.
Quiz: one of the Presidio's tenants makes some of the most famous movies in the world. George Lucas built his company's headqu

item.title: 31. Golden Gate Park: a park built on sand dunes
item.description:
Nineteenth Avenue cuts right through Golden Gate Park. It's 1,017 acres, and gets about 24 million visitors a year.
Quiz: before the park was built in the 1870s, what do you think covered three-quarters of this land? … Sand dunes! This whole western side of the city was called the Outside Lands. Engineer William Hammond Hall and gardener John McLaren spent years planting grasses and trees to hold the sand in place. Hall later became California's first state engineer, and designed flood control for the Sacramento Valley, where this whole trip began.
At the ocean end there are two Dutch-style

item.title: 32. Yerba Buena, the Gold Rush, and a city built on ships
item.description:
Welcome to San Francisco! Quick question: was this city always called San Francisco? … Nope! It was a little trading settlement called Yerba Buena, Spanish for good herb. In January 1847, the American mayor renamed it San Francisco, after the mission founded here in 1776. And here's a callback for you: one reason was that General Vallejo was planning a town called Francisca, after his wife. San Francisco grabbed the name first, so Vallejo's town became Benicia instead, after his wife's middle name.
In 1847 the town had about 459 people. Then gold was found, and it went from about 1,000 people

item.title: 33. 5:12 a.m., April 18, 1906
item.description:
Okay, let's talk about the morning San Francisco fell down. At 5:12 a.m. on the 18th of April, 1906, the San Andreas Fault ruptured along about 280 miles of the coast. That's the same fault we followed past Tomales Bay and Bolinas this morning. A foreshock hit first, and then the main shaking lasted about 42 seconds. Magnitude about 7.9.
Then came the fires, which burned for days. More than 3,000 people died, the deadliest earthquake in American history, and over 80 percent of the city was destroyed. At the time, San Francisco was the biggest city on the West Coast.
Quiz: for years people th

item.title: 34. Daly City: little boxes on the hillside
item.description:
We're crossing into Daly City. After the 1906 earthquake, thousands of homeless San Franciscans headed south to the ranches here, including a big one belonging to John Daly, a dairyman who'd married his boss's daughter. The town grew from those refugees and took his name.
Then, from the late 1940s, a developer called Henry Doelger built Westlake, one of the first big planned suburbs, with rows and rows of similar houses up the hillsides. Quiz: Westlake inspired a famous 1962 folk song by Malvina Reynolds, poking fun at rows of identical suburban houses. What's it called? … Little Boxes!

item.title: 35. Colma: where the dead outnumber the living
item.description:
Here's the weirdest town on our whole trip: Colma. Most of its land is cemeteries.
In 1900, San Francisco banned new burials inside the city, and in 1912 it evicted most of its existing cemeteries. So about 150,000 bodies were dug up and moved down here, at ten dollars per grave. Nearly everyone famous who died in San Francisco ended up here.
Quiz: the dead here outnumber the living. By roughly how much? … About a thousand to one! Somewhere around one and a half million people are buried here. It's been called the City of the Silent, and its unofficial motto is: It's great to be alive in Col

item.title: 36. Discovering San Francisco Bay
item.description:
On the hills to the west is Sweeney Ridge. And something big happened up there.
In 1769, the Spanish explorer Gaspar de Portolá was leading an expedition up the coast. He sent a scouting party, led by Sergeant José Ortega, north to find the Point Reyes headlands, which we drove past this morning. Ortega came back and reported he couldn't get there. Quiz: why not? … Because the Golden Gate was in the way! He'd found the strait. And from Sweeney Ridge, on the 4th of November 1769, the expedition became the first Europeans known to see San Francisco Bay. Well, the scouts had actually spotted it

item.title: 37. SFO: from cow pasture to the world
item.description:
And here we are: San Francisco International Airport. Quiz, one last time: when the city opened its airport here in May 1927, what was the land being used for? … It was a cow pasture! 150 acres, leased from the Mills family estate, as a temporary, experimental airport called Mills Field. In 1931 the city bought the land and named it San Francisco Airport, and international was added after World War Two. Pan Am moved its flying boats here in 1944. Funny detail: it's owned by San Francisco, but it's actually in San Mateo County.
So, Julia, Adam, our heroic driver: that's a wrap! From Sacramento
